name: OS Credential Dumping
summary: OS credential dumping is when an attacker pulls account login material out of a computer. This is usually a password hash, sometimes a clear text password. The attacker can then use it to move to other systems and reach restricted information.

name: Data from Local System
summary: Data from local system is when an attacker searches a computer they already control to find files and other data worth taking. This usually happens before the data is sent out of the network. It can cover documents, settings files, databases and more.

name: Remote Services
summary: Remote Services is when an attacker uses a valid account to log in to a service built for remote access, such as SSH, RDP or VNC. Once in, the attacker can act as that user. It is a common way to move from one system to another inside a network.

name: Obfuscated Files or Information
summary: Obfuscated Files or Information is a technique where an attacker hides the real content of a file, program or command by encrypting, encoding or packing it. The goal is to slip past security tools and make analysis harder. Tools look for known patterns, so changing how content looks can stop the patterns matching while it still runs.

name: Masquerading
summary: Masquerading is when an attacker changes how a file, program, service or account looks so it seems legitimate. They may change its name, where it sits or its descriptive details. The aim is to avoid being noticed by people and by security tools.

name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
summary: Exfiltration over a C2 channel is when an attacker sends stolen data out through the same channel they already use to control the infected system. The data is hidden inside what looks like normal control traffic, so no second route out of the network is needed. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1041 under Exfiltration.

name: Scheduled Task/Job
summary: Scheduled Task/Job is a technique where an attacker uses the task scheduling feature built into an operating system. The feature runs a program or script at a set time or on a repeat. Attackers use it to start malicious code, to keep their access after a restart, or to run code with higher privileges.

name: Process Injection
summary: Process injection is when an attacker runs their own code inside another program that is already running. The code then borrows the identity of that program. This can help it avoid security tools and, in some cases, gain more access.

name: Input Capture
summary: Input capture is when an attacker records what a user types or enters, to steal passwords or other information. It can happen silently in the background or by tricking the user into typing into a fake prompt or page. MITRE lists four forms: keylogging, GUI input capture, web portal capture and credential API hooking.

name: Process Discovery
summary: Process Discovery is a technique where attackers list the programs running on a system. The result tells them what software is present and helps them decide what to do next, for example whether to fully infect the target. MITRE tracks it as T1057 under the Discovery tactic.

name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
summary: Command and Scripting Interpreter is a technique where an attacker uses the built-in shells and scripting languages of a system to run commands, scripts or programs. Most systems already include these tools, so the activity can look like normal administration.

name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
summary: Exploitation for privilege escalation is when an attacker uses a flaw in software to gain higher permissions than they started with. For example, they may go from a normal user account to full control of the system. The flaw can be in the operating system, in software running with higher permissions, or in a signed driver. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1068.

name: Indicator Removal
summary: Indicator Removal is a technique where an attacker deletes or changes the traces that their activity leaves behind. These traces include logs, command histories and file details. The aim is to blend in with normal activity and make the intrusion harder to spot.

name: Application Layer Protocol
summary: Application Layer Protocol is a technique where attackers talk to a system they control using ordinary network protocols, such as those used for web browsing, file transfer, email or DNS. Because the traffic looks like normal traffic, it is harder to spot and block. MITRE tracks it as T1071 under the Command and Control tactic.

name: Valid Accounts
tactic: Stealth, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Initial Access
summary: Valid Accounts means an attacker logs in with real credentials that were stolen or bought. Because the login is genuine, the activity can look like a normal user. MITRE says the access can be used to get in, stay in the network, gain higher privileges or avoid detection, so defenders watch how an account behaves.

name: System Information Discovery
summary: System Information Discovery is when an attacker collects details about a device, such as its operating system version, patch level and hardware. The attacker uses this to decide what to do next on that device. It is a Discovery technique in MITRE ATT&CK.

name: File and Directory Discovery
summary: File and Directory Discovery is a technique where an attacker lists files and folders on a system or a network share to learn what is there. The results help the attacker decide what to do next, such as which data to take.

name: Account Discovery
summary: Account Discovery is when an attacker builds a list of valid accounts, usernames or email addresses on a system or inside a compromised environment. Knowing which accounts exist helps them plan what to do next. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as a Discovery technique.

name: Ingress Tool Transfer
summary: Ingress Tool Transfer is a technique where attackers bring tools or other files from outside into a network they have already broken into. The files are used for later steps of the attack. They can arrive through the attacker's control channel, FTP or other protocols, often using utilities the operating system already includes. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1105.

name: Modify Registry
summary: Modify Registry is a technique where an attacker changes settings in the Windows Registry. The Registry holds configuration for the system and its software. Changes can help an attacker stay on a machine, hide data or weaken security settings. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1112 under Defense Impairment and Persistence.

name: External Remote Services
summary: External Remote Services is a technique where an attacker uses a remote access service that faces the internet, such as a VPN or Citrix, to enter a network or to keep access to it. These services exist so staff can reach internal systems from outside. An attacker who gets valid logins can use them in the same way.

name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
summary: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information is a technique where attackers unpack, decode or decrypt content they had hidden earlier, so it can be used on the target system. The malware itself or built-in system utilities can do the work. MITRE tracks it as T1140 under the Stealth tactic.

name: Drive-by Compromise
summary: Drive-by Compromise is a way for attackers to gain access to a computer when a person visits a website during normal browsing. The site, or something it loads, delivers malicious code to the browser. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as an Initial Access technique.

name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
summary: Exploit Public-Facing Application is when an attacker abuses a weakness in a system that is reachable from the Internet to get into a network. The weakness can be a software bug, a temporary glitch or a misconfiguration. It is an Initial Access technique.

name: Compromise Software Supply Chain
summary: Compromise Software Supply Chain is a way for attackers to reach many computers through software they already trust. They change an application before it gets to the user, for example in its source code, its update system or its download. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as an Initial Access technique.

name: User Execution
summary: User Execution is when an attacker gets a person to run malicious code for them. The person might open a file, click a link or turn on a remote access tool without knowing the risk. It is an Execution technique in MITRE ATT&CK.

name: ClickFix: Malicious Copy and Paste (T1204.004)
summary: Malicious Copy and Paste lets an attacker run code without an exploit and without a browser download. The user pastes the command into a terminal or the Windows Run box. MITRE names ClickFix, where a fake error or CAPTCHA tells the user to do exactly that, as one such strategy.

name: Data Encrypted for Impact
summary: Data Encrypted for Impact is when attackers encrypt files or whole systems so the owner can no longer use them, and then hold back the key. It is the core step of ransomware. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as an Impact technique.

name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion
summary: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion is when malware checks whether it is running inside a virtual machine or an analysis sandbox, and changes what it does if it is. The aim is to avoid being studied. MITRE lists it under both Stealth and Discovery.

name: Server Software Component: Web Shell (T1505.003)
summary: A web shell is a small script that an attacker places on a web server. It lets the attacker run commands on that server from a distance. Because it sits on the server itself, it keeps working even if the first way in is closed, which is why attackers use it to keep access to the network over time.

name: Python Startup Hooks: .pth and sitecustomize.py Persistence (T1546.018)
summary: Python Startup Hooks let an attacker run code every time Python starts. A file dropped into the Python packages folder is processed by the interpreter itself, so the code runs even if the program never imports anything from it. MITRE tracks this as T1546.018.

name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
summary: Boot or logon autostart execution is when an attacker sets up a computer so that their program starts by itself when the system boots or a user logs on. This lets the attacker stay on the system after a restart. Some of these startup items run with higher privileges, so it can also help the attacker gain more control.

name: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
summary: Windows can start programs on its own when a user logs in. Attackers add their own program to the places that control this, the Registry run keys or the Startup folder. The program then starts again after every restart or logon.

name: Credentials in Files: Stealing Secrets from Config Files (T1552.001)
summary: Credentials in Files means an attacker reads passwords, keys and tokens that sit in ordinary files on a disk or a file share. Config files, .env files and cloud credential files are common targets. The stolen secret is then used to sign in somewhere else. MITRE tracks it as T1552.001.

name: Credentials from Password Stores
summary: Credentials from password stores is when an attacker looks in the places where passwords are saved and takes the logins they find. These places include system password storage, saved browser logins, password managers and cloud secrets vaults. Stolen logins can then be used to move to other systems.

name: Archive Collected Data
summary: Archive collected data is when an attacker packs stolen files into compressed or encrypted bundles before sending them out. This makes the data smaller and harder for a defender to read or notice. The attacker can use a utility already on the system, a third party library or a custom method. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1560 under Collection.

name: Hide Artifacts
summary: Hide Artifacts is a technique where attackers hide the traces of their activity, such as files, folders, user accounts or running tasks. The aim is to avoid being noticed by users and security tools. Attackers abuse operating system features that already hide items, so what is hidden is harder to find during a routine check. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1564.

name: Phishing (T1566): ATT&CK Technique
summary: Phishing is when an attacker sends a message that tricks someone into opening a malicious file, following a link or giving away a password. It is a common first step into a network. Defenders check attachments and links before delivery, use multi-factor authentication and make it easy for staff to report suspicious messages.

name: Encrypted Channel
summary: Encrypted Channel is a technique where attackers encrypt the traffic they use to control a compromised system. The encryption hides what is being sent, so security tools that read network traffic see only scrambled data. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1573 under Command and Control, and lists Emotet, gh0st RAT and NETWIRE as using it.

name: DLL
summary: DLL hijacking is when an attacker abuses the shared library files (DLLs) that Windows programs load. A trusted program is made to load a harmful DLL instead of, or alongside, the real one. This helps the attacker stay in place, gain higher privileges and avoid detection.

name: Reflective Code Loading
summary: Reflective code loading is a way for malware to run a program straight from memory, without starting a new process or putting the program on disk as a normal file. The payload can stay encrypted until the moment it runs. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as a Stealth technique.
